docs.title: What Argus finds
docs.text:
Stopped instances still charging

EC2, GCE, and Azure VMs that are stopped but still paying for reserved storage and EIPs.

Orphaned volumes and disks

EBS volumes, GCP Persistent Disks, and Azure Managed Disks with zero I/O for weeks.

Idle load balancers and NAT gateways

Resources processing zero bytes per day but billed by the hour.

Right-sizing opportunities

RDS db.r5.4xlarge at 4% CPU? EC2 m5.4xlarge with zero traffic? Argus names the current instance type and recommends the exact smaller tier — not "consider downsizing."

Over-provisioned clusters and caches

EKS, GKE, and AKS node groups, ElastiCache clusters, and Redshift nodes running at single-digit utilization — with specific node count and instance type recommendations.

Untagged and unowned resources

Resources with no owner tag that nobody knows about — prime deletion candidates.

Interactive chat mode

Ask questions in plain English: "Which RDS instances have been idle for 30+ days?" Argus investigates live and answers with costs and recommendations.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1 Discover

The cloud's asset inventory returns every billable resource across all regions, costs are fetched in one batched call, and the list is sorted by cost so the most expensive candidates are investigated first.

→ 2 Investigate

A ReAct agent loop reasons like a human analyst — pulling metrics over your lookback window (90 days by default), actual spend, and last-activity timestamps only for resources where it matters. No hardcoded thresholds.

→ 3 Report

Prioritized findings land in Slack (or Teams, or any webhook) with exact dollar amounts and specific actions — delete, right-size, or tag for review. Or skip the batch scan and ask questions live with argus chat.

Argus uses a ReAct agent loop — the AI decides what to investigate, calls the right tools in the right order, and reasons about idleness qualitatively. No hardcoded thresholds. No rules per resource type. The same brain works across all three clouds.

docs.title: Design principlesReady to find what's wasting money?
docs.text:
Principle What it means Same brain, different hands core/ is pure Python — zero cloud imports. Adapters are the only place SDKs live. AI drives the analysis No hardcoded idle thresholds. Claude reasons about each resource in context. Least privilege always Read-only IAM roles. No write permissions ever requested. Batch everything Costs fetched in one batched call before the AI starts; the AI conversation is capped by MAX_AGENT_ITERATIONS and LLM_BUDGET_USD. Cost control by design. Fail loudly Typed exceptions from adapters. Failed accounts are logged and listed in the report's scan_errors; a failed delivery exits non-zero.

What a scan costs

Model cost is capped by LLM_BUDGET_USD (default $2.00) and shown before the model runs. One measured run on 1,614 resources cost about $1.4 to $1.55 on Bedrock; see scan cost. Dollar figures in a report are labelled billed, list price or model estimate, and an estimate is not a savings figure.

Clone, configure, deploy. First scan in under 5 minutes. Free and open source.

This page is the current status of Argus as of v0.7.0: what has shipped, what is known to be incomplete, and what is planned next. It is the single source of truth for project status; older planning documents have been retired. No dates are promised; items ship when they're ready and well-tested.

docs.title: Shipped in v0.7.0
docs.text:
A trust release. Contains breaking changes; see the changelog.

  • Honest money. Dollars are labelled billed, list price or model estimate; with no billed data the headline says "unverified waste estimate".
  • Coverage, preflight and loud failure. Reports state what was analysed and what was not; AWS preflight runs before any model spend; failed scans exit 3 or 4.
  • Guards. A missing metric is "could not judge", not idle; ElastiCache failover replicas and AMI-backed or retained snapshots are not recommended for deletion.
  • Decision board is the only HTML report. PDF export is removed. argus board --client-safe writes a redacted copy for clients.
  • Depth differs by cloud. AWS is the proven path; GCP and Azure have no state rules, preflight or tag fallback yet.

docs.title: Shipped in v0.6.0
docs.text:
A safety release for the remediation path. Contains a breaking change; see the changelog.

  • Automatic tickets are opt-in. Scheduled scans create Jira tickets only when REMEDIATION_ENABLED=true (default false). argus policies apply --confirm is unchanged.
  • Dry runs never touch Jira. DRY_RUN=true / argus scan --dry-run previously still created real tickets when Jira was configured. Dry runs now only log what would be tracked.
  • One summary line per run. remediation_summary findings=… proposals=… tracked=… failed=… dry_run=…, plus error_type on every failure so a Jira outage can be told apart from a bug.
  • One policy-folder setting. The CLI and scheduled scans now both read ARGUS_POLICY_DIR (the older ARGUS_POLICIES_DIR still works).
  • Policy excludes work as documented. Matching any exclude tag entry now skips the resource, so the bundled environment: prod and argus-exempt: "true" excludes each work on their own (before, a resource needed both tags to be skipped).
  • accounts scope filters work. Findings now record the account/project/subscription they came from.
  • No repeat Jira comments. An unchanged finding no longer adds a comment to its ticket on every re-scan.

docs.title: Resource Registry
docs.text: Each of the 114 supported resource types is now declared once — discovery query, metric names, cost key, display name — and the agent prompt, report, and chat mode all read from it automatically. Adding a new type is a one-file change.

docs.title: Remediation v1 — Policy-driven Jira tickets
docs.text:
Argus finds waste and now also creates Jira tickets for matched findings automatically.

  • Write a YAML policy file per resource type (see config/policies.example/)
  • Argus evaluates findings against your policies after every scan (opt-in since v0.6.0 via REMEDIATION_ENABLED=true)
  • A Jira ticket is opened for each match — deduplication prevents re-creating tickets for the same resource on the next scan
  • If the AI's analysis changes (cost drifts, priority changes), Argus adds a comment to the existing ticket rather than opening a duplicate
  • Ticket URLs are posted to Slack alongside the waste digest so nothing gets lost
  • Full audit log (audit.jsonl) of every ticket created

What Remediation v1 does not do: auto-execute cloud commands. Argus proposes; your team acts. Auto-remediation (approval gate → executor service) is Remediation v2 — see below.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
Small, known issues in what has shipped. Not scheduled; contributions welcome.

  • Slack ticket count wording. The digest says "N remediation ticket(s) created", but N includes existing tickets that were only updated or left unchanged.
  • No decision tracing. There is no trace of the agent's tool calls and reasoning per finding (Langfuse-style). Debugging a wrong "idle" call relies on logs and the report's AI reasoning text.
  • Logs, not metrics. Remediation outcomes are structured log lines only; there are no counters exported to CloudWatch / Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor.
  • SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL is always required. Startup validation insists on it (unless DRY_RUN=true) even when NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER only lists teams or webhook.
  • GCP deploy script doesn't enable the Vertex AI API even though Vertex AI is the default provider on Cloud Run.
  • Bundled policies aren't in the PyPI package. pip install users don't get config/policies/; copy it from the repository (or write your own) and point ARGUS_POLICY_DIR at it.

docs.title: Remediation v2 — Auto-execution
docs.text:
Status: planned, not started. Everything below this line is future work; none of it is in v0.7.0.

The problem: Remediation v1 (shipped in v0.5.0, made opt-in in v0.6.0) creates tickets. Acting on them still requires manual work.

What changes:

  • Jira ticket approval triggers a webhook to a dedicated executor service
  • Executor carries out the action (stop, resize, delete) using a write-scoped IAM role
  • Argus itself stays strictly read-only — the executor is a separate, scoped component
  • Full rollback support for reversible actions (stop → can restart, snapshot → preserved)
  • Guardrails: dry-run mode, per-action confirmation window, automatic revert on anomaly

Why it's not in v1: write-scoped execution requires a separate trust boundary and a much higher bar for testing. Building it half-finished would be worse than not building it.

docs.title: Historical Tracking
docs.text:
Already shipped: each report compares against the previous scan — findings are marked new or recurring, and scan_diff counts new, recurring, and resolved findings.

The problem: that comparison only looks one scan back and isn't surfaced in the digest, so it's hard to see whether waste is trending down or the same resources keep coming back.

What changes:

  • Resources flagged repeatedly surface with a "flagged N times" badge
  • Weekly digest includes "X findings resolved since last week, saving $Y/mo"

docs.title: Owner Routing
docs.text:
The problem: a single Slack channel becomes noise when findings span multiple teams.

What changes:

  • Route findings to per-team channels based on resource tags (owner=platform, team=data-eng)
  • Configurable suppression rules and repeated-finding escalation
  • Requires consistent tagging hygiene across the account to be effective

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
The problem: accessing Argus requires the CLI or a Slack digest — not useful inside AI-first workflows.

What changes:

  • Expose Argus as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server
  • Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client can query your cloud costs live
  • REST API exposed alongside for integration with PagerDuty, Jira, and custom dashboards

Suggesting features

If one of these matters more to you than another, say so in GitHub Discussions — it influences prioritization.

docs.title: Why we use a ReAct loop instead of rules for idle resource detection
docs.text:
Most cloud cost tools work off rules. If CPU stays below 5% for seven days, flag the instance as idle. If a volume has zero read operations for thirty days, flag it as unused. These rules are simple, fast, and easy to audit. We tried this approach first when building Argus. It kept getting things wrong.

This post explains what the problem actually is, what a ReAct loop is, and the specific tradeoffs we accepted by going down this path.

Updated 2026-09-27 for v0.6.0

A few details below changed since this was written: Argus now discovers and cost-sorts resources before the AI starts (so the AI sees the top 200 by cost, with costs attached), the metrics window defaults to 90 days, and a scan is a multi-turn AI conversation rather than a single call. The text has been corrected where it described those mechanics.

docs.title: What rules look like in practice
docs.text:
Here is a small slice of what a rule-based idle detector needs to handle for just five resource types:

Resource Rule EC2 instance CPU < 5% for 7 days RDS instance connections = 0 for 14 days NAT Gateway bytes transferred < 1 MB/day Lambda function invocations < 10/month EBS volume read/write ops = 0 for 30 days

This looks manageable until you add more resource types. AWS alone has over 200 resource types that can show up in a real account. GCP and Azure add hundreds more. Each one needs its own rule, its own metric, its own threshold, and its own exception list.

But the bigger problem is not scale. It is that "idle" is context-dependent in ways a static rule cannot express.

docs.title: The context problem
docs.text:
Take a NAT Gateway moving 500 KB per day. The rule says: flag it, that is too low. But:

  • Is it a VPN tunnel that carries low-volume management traffic to on-premise systems? Then it is not idle, it is load-bearing.
  • Is it attached to a subnet with no active instances since a migration six months ago? Then it is completely orphaned.
  • Does it have an environment=prod tag and an owner from the platform team? Different action than one tagged environment=dev with no owner.

The bytes metric alone cannot tell you which scenario you are in. You need to look at the routing table, the subnet, the tag, the CloudTrail history, and the cost trend together. A rule cannot do that. It can only look at one metric at a time.

This is not a corner case. It comes up constantly in real accounts. The monthly reporting job that runs once a month and looks idle every other week. The RDS read replica that has zero connections because it exists as a failover, not for active use. The Lambda function invoked three times a month that sends critical billing notifications.

Rules have no way to distinguish these from genuinely dead resources. So they either produce false positives that erode trust, or you add so many exceptions that the rules stop doing anything useful.

docs.title: What a ReAct loop is
docs.text:
ReAct stands for Reason and Act. It is a pattern for AI agents where the model alternates between reasoning about what to do next and calling a tool to gather more information.

In Argus, the loop works like this:

  1. Before the AI starts, Argus discovers every billable resource, fetches costs in one batched call, and keeps the most expensive ones (200 by default). The AI receives that list with types, regions, names, and monthly cost already attached.
  2. It picks a resource that looks worth investigating and calls get_metrics() to fetch CloudWatch data (the last 90 days by default).
  3. It reads the metrics, adds them to its context, and decides whether to look further. It might call get_last_activity() to check CloudTrail for the last time a human or system touched it.
  4. It keeps going until it has enough information to make a judgment, then writes a finding in plain language with its reasoning, a cost estimate, and a recommendation.

The loop exits when the AI decides it has investigated enough resources. It does not need to check every resource. It reasons about which ones warrant deeper investigation, the same way a senior engineer would skim a list of resources and immediately know which ones to look at first.

docs.title: How signals combine
docs.text:
Here is a concrete example of what this looks like for a single resource:

The AI sees all five signals together. It knows that 847 bytes of network traffic over two weeks is essentially nothing. It knows that 73 days without human activity is a long time. It knows $94.20 per month is real money. It knows the team=backend tag means it should call out the owner. No single signal would have been enough. Together, they add up to a clear finding.

A rule checking bytes transferred would have flagged this correctly, but it would have also flagged the VPN tunnel next to it. Argus doesn't read routing tables, but the AI weighs the signals it does have (tags, names, owner, last activity, cost) and can say "low traffic but owned and recently touched, ask the platform team" instead of "delete". A single-metric rule cannot.

docs.title: The actual tradeoffs
docs.text:
This approach is not free. Here is what we gave up:

Determinism. Two scans of the same account might produce slightly different findings if resource states are borderline. We set temperature=0 and prompt the model to cite specific metrics in every finding, which makes its reasoning auditable and significantly reduces variance. But it is not zero.

Speed. The agent loop takes longer than a rule check. Rules run in milliseconds. A full Argus scan takes two to four minutes depending on account size. For a weekly report this is fine. For something you want to run on every deployment it is not.

Cost. Each scan is a bounded, multi-turn AI conversation, capped by an iteration limit and a per-scan dollar budget (LLM_BUDGET_USD, $2 by default). On AWS we use Bedrock. A typical scan costs around $0.24 in API usage. Across 52 weeks that is about $12.50 per year per account. For the context: a single overlooked idle NAT Gateway costs $32/month.

Debuggability. When a rule fires, you know exactly why. When the AI flags a resource, you have to read its reasoning. We require the AI to include specific metric values in every finding, so you can verify the logic. But it is more work to audit than a threshold check.

What we got in return: we do not write rules. We do not maintain thresholds per resource type. We do not build exception lists. The same agent works across AWS, GCP, and Azure without any cloud-specific idle logic. When AWS releases a new resource type, the agent can reason about it immediately using whatever metrics are available, without any code changes.

docs.title: What this means if you want to extend Argus
docs.text:
The core of Argus is the agent loop in core/agent/loop.py. It calls four methods on a cloud adapter: list_resources, get_metrics, get_cost, and get_last_activity. That is the full contract.

If you want to add a new cloud, you implement those four methods, register its resource types, and add a thin entrypoint (see Adding a Cloud Adapter). If you want to improve the analysis, you edit the system prompt in core/agent/prompts.py. The agent loop itself doesn't change.

The adapter pattern and the AI reasoning are deliberately separated so that each can be swapped out independently. You could replace Claude with GPT-4o or Gemini by implementing a different AI provider. You could add a new cloud by writing a new adapter. The core loop stays the same either way.

If you want to try it on your own account, the quickstart takes about ten minutes. The source is on GitHub. Feedback and PRs welcome.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Understand how Argus works under the hood.

  • How It Works — the ReAct agent loop, tool dispatch, and finding lifecycle
  • AI Reasoning — how Claude decides what's idle vs. active
  • Cloud Adapters — the four-method contract and how each cloud implements it
  • AI Providers — Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI

docs.title: Cloud Adapters
docs.text: Every cloud adapter implements the same four-method contract defined in adapters/base.py. The agent loop never calls cloud SDKs directly — it only calls these methods.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
class CloudAdapter(ABC):

    def list_resources(
        self,
        ignore_regions: list[str] | None = None,
    ) -> list[Resource]:
        """Return every billable resource, excluding ignored regions."""

    def get_metrics(
        self,
        resource_id: str,
        resource_type: str,
        days: int = 90,
    ) -> MetricSummary:
        """Return usage metrics for the past N days."""

    def get_cost(
        self,
        resource_ids: list[str],
        days: int = 30,
    ) -> dict[str, float]:
        """Return USD cost per resource. Always called with all IDs at once."""

    def get_last_activity(
        self,
        resource_id: str,
        resource_type: str,
    ) -> datetime | None:
        """Return the last meaningful activity timestamp, or None."""

docs.title: Resource and MetricSummary types
docs.text:
@dataclass
class Resource:
    resource_id: str        # ARN / full resource path / Azure resource ID
    resource_type: str      # e.g. "AWS::EC2::Instance"
    cloud: str              # "aws" | "gcp" | "azure"
    region: str
    name: str | None = None # from Name tag or display name
    tags: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

@dataclass
class MetricSummary:
    resource_id: str
    resource_type: str
    period_days: int                 # lookback window used (METRICS_LOOKBACK_DAYS, default 90)
    metrics: dict[str, Any]          # metric_name → aggregated value over the window
    has_data: bool = True            # False if no CloudWatch/Monitoring data exists

docs.title: Non-billable resource filter (AWS)
docs.text:
list_resources filters out types that never appear on an AWS bill before returning results:

  • All AWS::IAM::* (roles, policies, users, groups)
  • EC2 primitives: subnets, route tables, network ACLs, DHCP options, internet gateways
  • CloudFormation stacks and stacksets
  • SSM parameters, documents, patch baselines
  • Config rules and recorders, Lambda event source mappings and layer versions, SNS subscriptions, CloudWatch alarms
  • And more — see adapters/aws/resource_explorer.py

This cuts 60–70% of the resource list before the AI sees it.

docs.text: Argus supports four AI providers. All implement the same AIProvider interface — swapping providers requires only changing AI_PROVIDER in your environment.

docs.title: Anthropic API
docs.text:
The universal fallback — works on any cloud, best for local development.

AI_PROVIDER=anthropic
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

Features: - Prompt caching (cache_control: ephemeral) on the system prompt — iterations 2–N are billed at the cached-read rate for that portion - Exponential backoff on rate-limit and server errors (up to 3 attempts, 1s then 2s)

docs.title: AWS Bedrock
docs.text:
The default in production AWS deployments. Uses the Lambda execution role — no API key.

AI_PROVIDER=bedrock
BEDROCK_MODEL_ID=anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6   # optional
BEDROCK_REGION=us-east-1                        # optional

Requirements: - Bedrock must be enabled in BEDROCK_REGION - Model access must be enabled: Bedrock console → Model catalog → Claude Sonnet → Enable - Lambda execution role needs bedrock:InvokeModel - Some newer Claude models cannot be called with a bare model id. If Bedrock rejects BEDROCK_MODEL_ID, set it to the inference profile id or ARN for your region (copy it from the Bedrock console), and allow bedrock:InvokeModel on that profile - AWS account must have a valid payment method (Bedrock returns INVALID_PAYMENT_INSTRUMENT otherwise — see Troubleshooting)

Features: - Exponential backoff on ThrottlingException (up to 3 attempts, 1s then 2s) - Automatic retry for models that reject temperature (for example newer Claude models): Argus retries once without it, remembers this for the rest of the run, and logs a warning. Dropping it does not count against the throttling retries. Other validation errors, including an out-of-range temperature, still fail immediately.

docs.title: Vertex AI (Gemini)
docs.text:
The default for GCP Cloud Run deployments.

AI_PROVIDER=vertexai
VERTEXAI_PROJECT=my-gcp-project
VERTEXAI_LOCATION=us-central1    # optional
VERTEXAI_MODEL=google/gemini-1.5-pro-002  # optional

Authentication: Uses Google Application Default Credentials. - On Cloud Run: automatically uses the service account attached to the job - Locally: gcloud auth application-default login

Features: - Uses the OpenAI-compatible Vertex AI endpoint — no extra SDK dependency - Automatic credential refresh when token expires (1-hour TTL) - Exponential backoff on rate limits

Always include the publisher prefix in VERTEXAI_MODEL

The OpenAI-compatible Vertex AI endpoint requires a publisher/model format. Use google/gemini-2.5-flash, not gemini-2.5-flash — the bare model name returns 400 Malformed publisher model.

docs.title: Azure OpenAI (GPT-4o)
docs.text:
The default for Azure Function deployments.

AI_PROVIDER=azure_openai
AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT=https://my-resource.openai.azure.com/
AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT=gpt-4o        # optional
AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION=2024-10-21   # optional
# For local dev without az login:
AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY=...

Authentication: - In production: DefaultAzureCredential — picks up managed identity automatically - Locally: either az login (recommended) or set AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY

Features: - Wraps AuthenticationError into a friendly EnvironmentError with setup instructions - Exponential backoff on rate limits - Automatic retry for reasoning model restrictions: if the deployment rejects max_tokens or temperature, Argus retries with max_completion_tokens and no temperature — no config change needed

Reasoning models (o1, o3, o4-mini):

Many subscriptions — especially newer or free-tier ones — can only deploy reasoning models. Two things to know:

Setting Standard models (gpt-4o) Reasoning models (o1/o3/o4-mini) AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION 2024-10-21 works Requires 2024-12-01-preview or later AI_TEMPERATURE Respected Silently dropped (Argus handles automatically) 
# Required when using o4-mini, o1, or o3 deployments
AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION=2024-12-01-preview

docs.title: The AIProvider interface
docs.text:
All providers implement one method:

class AIProvider(ABC):
    def chat(
        self,
        messages: list[Message],
        tools: list[Tool],
        system_prompt: str | None = None,
    ) -> AIResponse:
        ...

The agent loop calls chat() — it never knows which provider is underneath. See Adding an AI Provider to add your own.

docs.title: Why AI instead of thresholds?
docs.text:
Traditional cost tools use hardcoded rules:

# The old way — fragile, needs constant maintenance
if resource_type == "EC2" and cpu_avg < 5.0:
    flag_idle()
elif resource_type == "RDS" and connections_avg < 1.0:
    flag_idle()
elif resource_type == "NatGateway" and bytes_out == 0:
    flag_idle()
# ... 50 more elif blocks ...

This breaks immediately when: - A resource has unusual usage patterns - A new resource type is added - Context matters (a dev database with zero connections on weekends isn't idle)

Argus takes a different approach: give the AI the raw signal data and let it reason.

docs.title: What Claude receives
docs.text:
For each candidate resource, the AI has access to:

  • Cost — monthly USD from Cost Explorer / BigQuery / Cost Management, already attached to the resource list
  • Metrics — aggregated over METRICS_LOOKBACK_DAYS (default 90): CPU, network bytes, request count, IOPS, connections, etc.
  • Instance size (AWS) — current instance type/class injected alongside metrics (e.g. instance_type: db.r5.4xlarge, memory_mb: 3072)
  • Last activity — timestamp of the last meaningful CloudTrail / Audit Log event
  • Tags — owner, environment, team, purpose
  • Resource type and region — context for what the resource is supposed to do

docs.title: How Claude decides
docs.text:
Claude applies qualitative reasoning that adapts to context:

EC2 at 0.001% CPU

i-0abc is an EC2 t3.large instance with:
- CPUUtilization avg: 0.0014% (90-day average)
- NetworkIn avg: 0 bytes
- NetworkOut avg: 0 bytes
- Last CloudTrail event: null (no events in 90 days)
- Tags: {} (no owner, no environment)
- Cost: $28.40/month

Assessment: This instance is effectively idle.
A t3.large with 0.001% CPU and zero network traffic
is not serving any workload. The absence of any tags
suggests it may be a forgotten resource. No CloudTrail
activity in 90 days confirms no recent human interaction.

Priority: HIGH ($28.40/month, confirmed idle)
Recommendation: Terminate. If data is needed, take an
EBS snapshot first.

RDS with zero connections — but recent activity

db-prod-replica has:
- DatabaseConnections avg: 0.0
- CPUUtilization avg: 0.3%
- Last CloudTrail event: 2026-06-01T14:22:00Z (6 days ago)
- Tags: {"Environment": "prod", "Owner": "platform-team"}
- Cost: $45.00/month

Assessment: This RDS instance shows zero connections but
was modified 6 days ago by the platform team. It may be
a standby replica, a recently migrated instance, or be
used only during specific batch windows. The owner tag
indicates active ownership.

Priority: LOW (owned resource, recently touched)
Recommendation: Tag for review — ask the platform team
if this replica is still needed.

RIGHT-SIZE: RDS over-provisioned

db-analytics-01 is an RDS db.r5.4xlarge with:
- CPUUtilization avg: 4.2% (90-day average)
- DatabaseConnections avg: 2.1
- instance_type: db.r5.4xlarge
- multi_az: true
- engine: postgres 14.7
- storage_gb: 500
- Cost: $1,240/month

Assessment: This database is severely over-provisioned.
CPU at 4.2% and fewer than 3 concurrent connections over
90 days on a db.r5.4xlarge (128 GB RAM, 16 vCPUs) indicates
the workload could run comfortably on a db.r5.xlarge.
Multi-AZ is also enabled, doubling the instance cost on a
DB that is barely used.

Priority: HIGH ($1,240/month, clear right-sizing opportunity)
Recommendation: RIGHT-SIZE: db.r5.4xlarge → db.r5.xlarge
(~$900/month savings). Also evaluate disabling Multi-AZ
(~$620/month additional savings) if this is not a
production-critical database.

docs.title: Priority rules
docs.text:
The system prompt defines the priority framework:

Priority Condition HIGH Confirmed idle AND costs > $20/month MEDIUM Likely idle OR costs $5–$20/month LOW Possibly idle OR costs < $5/month

Claude applies these rules but also exercises judgment — a $3/month resource that is definitively orphaned (no tags, no activity, no owner) might still be flagged HIGH if there are many of them in the account.

docs.title: System prompt
docs.text:
The system prompt is built once per scan in core/agent/prompts.py:

  • Identifies the agent role and mission
  • Lists accounts and regions being scanned
  • Provides the investigation workflow (6 steps, starting from the cost-sorted resource list)
  • Defines what to look for (6 categories of waste) and right-sizing rules
  • Sets the priority rules and the valid actions per resource type
  • Enforces efficiency rules (use the cost_usd already in the list, focus on expensive candidates, don't over-investigate)
  • Enforces read-only behavior

With the Anthropic API provider, the prompt is pinned in Anthropic's prompt cache, so subsequent loop iterations reuse the cached version, cutting the cost of the multi-turn conversation.

docs.title: Baseline Rules
docs.text:
Argus asks the model to judge resources, but a few cases are obvious enough that the answer should not depend on the model's mood. These are deterministic baseline rules: they run before the model, over every discovered resource of the matching type (they ignore the MAX_RESOURCES_PER_SCAN cap), and their findings win over the model's for the same resource. Two runs on the same account therefore always agree on them.

The first three rules read CloudWatch metrics; the last three read the resource's current configuration with read-only EC2 Describe* calls (ec2:DescribeVolumes, ec2:DescribeAddresses, ec2:DescribeInstances). A rule only fires on data Argus actually received. A resource with no data, or a failed metrics call, is never reported by a rule (the model may still look at it, with low confidence).

Rule id Resource Fires when (over the metrics window) List price used nat-gateway-idle NAT gateway Under 1 MiB in and out combined $32.85/month alb-no-requests Application Load Balancer (ARN contains /app/) 0 requests and 0 active connections $16.43/month classic-elb-no-requests Classic Load Balancer 0 requests $18.25/month ebs-volume-unattached EBS volume State is available (not attached to anything) size x type price, for example 100 GiB gp3 = $8.00/month elastic-ip-unassociated Elastic IP Not associated with an instance or network interface $3.65/month ec2-instance-stopped EC2 instance State is stopped (its attached volumes still bill) sum of attached volumes; confidence medium, no finding if the cost is 0

List prices are us-east-1 hourly rates x 730 hours, excluding data processing. When Cost Explorer returns a billed cost for the resource, that replaces the list price and the finding's cost_basis is billed; otherwise it is estimated.

Each rule finding has detected_by: "rule:<id>", confidence: "high" (a window under 90 days caps it at medium), and a recommendation that tells you what to check before deleting (for example route tables that still point at a NAT gateway).

Rules are on by default. Set ARGUS_BASELINE_RULES=false to turn them off. Coverage counts a resource as analysed once a rule has evaluated it.

docs.title: Decision board
docs.text:
A scan can return hundreds of findings. The decision board turns a scan report into one page that groups them into opportunities and lets a person mark each one Approve, Investigate or Keep. It is a single HTML file: no server, no login, no network requests.

argus board --report local_reports/aws/2026/10/30/<scan>.json
# writes <scan>.board.html next to the report; --out chooses another path

It needs only the JSON report. It works with reports from earlier versions too, because the opportunities are rebuilt from the findings when a report has none. See a built example in examples/sample-board.html (made-up data; regenerate it with python examples/make_sample_board.py).

docs.title: What is on the page
docs.text:
Part What it shows Header The Argus logo and name, the page title, and the scan date, account count and finding count Tally (sticky) Approved a month, investigating, kept and undecided; export decisions, export CSV, import decisions, clear all Overview A "Read before deciding" banner when the scan reported warnings (for example no resource-level cost data); KPI cards (reported waste, opportunities, billed share, unpriced findings, resources analysed, cost of this run); where the money is (dollars by cost basis, and the Easy and Needs-an-owner lanes); cost of this run Decide A filter rail (lane, decision, action, search) and a grid of opportunity cards Kept on purpose Everything marked Keep, with its reason and expiry About this report Collapsed in the footer: scan id, schema version, coverage, definitions and limits

The layout uses the whole width: the cards flow into as many columns as fit, the filter rail sits beside them on wide screens and becomes a bar across the top on narrower ones.

docs.title: An opportunity card
docs.text: Each card carries a savings range (billed plus list-priced dollars up to adding the model's estimates) with a chip for every cost basis, its lane, action and confidence, a one-line risk, collapsible evidence and check-first steps, the full member list, and the owners found in tags. The text is built from templates and the members' own data, without a model.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Decision Meaning Approve You want this done. It counts in the approved total Investigate An owner should look first. It counts as "at stake", not as approved Keep It stays on purpose. A reason is required, and an optional date says until when

Decisions are stored in the browser (local storage) and are keyed by the opportunity's stable id, so they still apply to a later scan. To share them, export the decisions file and import it elsewhere; when the same opportunity was decided twice, the newer decision wins. The CSV export lists every opportunity with its range and decision; cells that start with =, +, - or @ are escaped so a spreadsheet cannot run them. Argus never changes a resource: approving here only records a decision.

docs.title: Cost of this run
docs.text: The KPI card and panel show what the scan cost to run, taken from the report: model spend against the budget and against the estimate made before the run, model calls and tokens, the cost per 1,000 resources analysed, and the billed and list-priced waste found per $1 of model spend. That last figure is waste found, not savings realized. The report does not record AWS API charges (for example Cost Explorer requests) or the cost of the place Argus runs, so those are not included.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The page sets a Content Security Policy that allows only its own inline style and script, by hash. There are no inline style attributes, no event-handler attributes, no images or fonts from outside, and no network requests. Every string that comes from the scan (names, tags, reasons) is escaped, and the embedded data cannot close its own script tag.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text: Native buttons, inputs and labels; toggle buttons expose their state; the tally, filter count and status line are polite live regions; a skip link; visible focus; reduced-motion support; light and dark themes (the #theme=dark or #theme=light URL fragment forces one). Colour pairs are tested for WCAG AA contrast, and the page was scanned with axe in both themes at five widths.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The action of an opportunity is read from the wording of each recommendation, so unusual wording falls back to Review.
  • Decisions live in one browser unless exported; there is no shared state.
  • Commitments (Savings Plans, reservations) are not analysed.
  • This static page is deliberately plain. A richer dashboard is planned for the product frontend.

docs.title: Client-safe copy
docs.text:
argus board --report <scan>.json --client-safe --hide-tags cost-centre,team
argus board --report <scan>.json --client-safe --hide-tags '*'

--client-safe writes a redacted copy and leaves the report untouched:

Hidden Becomes Account, project and subscription ids account-1, account-2, ... (stable within the report) AWS ARNs service:region:resource (partition and account removed) Cost of this run (KPI and panel) removed Caller identity check (who ran the scan) removed Tag keys named in --hide-tags, or all with * removed, owners lane updated

Resource names, types, regions, amounts and cost bases are kept. Redaction is pattern based: a client name typed into a resource name or tag value is not detected, so read the page before sending it.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Argus follows a clean separation of concerns called Same brain. Different hands. Different home.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  core/  — Pure Python, zero cloud imports                       │
│                                                                 │
│  AgentLoop.run()  (scan pipeline, the default engine)           │
│   ├── Discover: adapter.list_resources() + costs                │
│   ├── Decide by rule: idle NAT / ALB, unattached volumes, ...   │
│   ├── Gather evidence in code: metrics, config, last activity   │
│   └── Triage: batched, stateless model calls -> findings        │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
            ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
            ▼                  ▼                  ▼
     CloudAdapter          AIProvider         Entrypoint
     (AWS/GCP/Azure)   (Bedrock/Anthropic   (Lambda/CloudRun/
                        /Vertex/AzureOAI)    AzureFunction)

Brain = core/ — the agent loop and prompts. No cloud imports. Runs in any environment.

Hands = adapters/ — cloud-specific data collection. Implements a four-method contract.

Home = entrypoints/ — thin runtime wrappers. No business logic.

docs.title: The scan pipeline
docs.text:
A scan runs in five steps. Everything that is a fact is gathered in code; the model only judges.

  1. Discover. The adapter lists resources. On AWS, Resource Explorer types such as ec2:natgateway are mapped to the registry's ids, and free configuration objects (security-group rules, subnets, IAM roles, task definitions, ...) are skipped on purpose and counted in coverage.free_config_skipped.
  2. Decide by rule. Baseline rules flag the unambiguous cases (idle NAT gateways and load balancers from metrics; unattached volumes, unassociated Elastic IPs and stopped instances from configuration). They run over every resource, are priced from a list-price catalog, and win over the model.
  3. Gather evidence. For every remaining resource Argus collects metrics (over the configured window), cost, configuration, and, where metrics could not decide, last activity. Missing data stays missing; it is never turned into zero.
  4. Triage. Resources are ranked (billed cost, high-impact types first) and sent to the model in batches. Each batch is one stateless call, so spend grows linearly with the number of resources. Before the first call Argus estimates the cost; it stops before a batch that would overspend the budget and keeps everything found so far.
  5. Report. Findings carry their evidence, confidence, cost_basis and detected_by. The summary is generated from the findings, not by another model call.

Guards between triage and report. A model finding is withheld from the waste total, and listed under coverage.withheld, when the evidence cannot support it:

  • a traffic-based resource (NAT gateway, load balancer, WAF, VPN, Client VPN, Transit Gateway attachment, VPC endpoint) whose traffic metrics were unavailable or empty
  • an ElastiCache node in a replication group with automatic failover or Multi-AZ, or one whose replication settings could not be read
  • an EBS snapshot that an AMI uses, that a tag marks as retained or a safety copy, or whose details could not be read
  • a CloudWatch log group that received log events inside the activity window, or whose last event time could not be read (CloudTrail does not record log ingestion, so Argus reads the newest log stream)
  • an RDS or Aurora automated snapshot, an AWS Backup snapshot or a retained automated backup (managed by retention, not delete candidates), a snapshot a tag marks as retained, or one whose details could not be read

The guards apply to the default pipeline engine only. The react engine and argus chat do not have them.

ARGUS_ENGINE=react switches back to the original tool-calling loop described below, which also powers argus chat.

docs.title: The ReAct loop (chat and the react engine)
docs.text:
Argus uses ReAct (Reason + Act) — a pattern where the AI alternates between reasoning and tool use.

Before the AI sees anything, a Phase 0 step runs without AI tokens: it discovers all resources, drops non-billable types and anything matching EXCLUDE_TAGS / EXCLUDE_RESOURCE_TYPES, fetches cost for all of them in one batched call, sorts by cost, and keeps the top MAX_RESOURCES_PER_SCAN (default 200). The AI's first list_resources call returns that pre-sorted list with cost_usd already attached.

User:      "Begin your cloud cost analysis now."

Claude:    <thinks> I'll start by listing all resources.
           <calls>  list_resources()

Tool:      [{"id":"i-0abc","type":"AWS::EC2::Instance","region":"us-east-1","cost_usd":28.4},
            {"id":"nat-0def","type":"AWS::EC2::NatGateway","region":"us-east-1","cost_usd":10.8},
            ...]   # already sorted by cost, capped at 200

Claude:    <thinks> i-0abc costs $28.40/month. Let me check if it's actually being used.
           <calls>  get_metrics(resource_id="i-0abc", resource_type="AWS::EC2::Instance")
                    get_last_activity(resource_id="i-0abc", resource_type="AWS::EC2::Instance")

Tool:      {"has_data": true, "CPUUtilization_avg": 0.0014, "NetworkIn_avg": 0.0}
           null

Claude:    <thinks> No CloudTrail events in 90 days + near-zero metrics = idle.
           ... investigates more resources ...
           <calls>  submit_findings([...])

When the AI requests several tools in one turn, they run in parallel. The loop runs for up to MAX_AGENT_ITERATIONS (default 50) and stops early if the scan's LLM_BUDGET_USD is reached.

docs.title: Tool dispatch
docs.text:
AgentLoop._execute() maps tool names to adapter calls. Only these five tools are allowed; anything else is rejected before execution:

Tool Adapter method Returns list_resources (Phase 0 result, cached) Top resources by cost, compact JSON with cost_usd get_metrics adapter.get_metrics(resource_id, resource_type, days) MetricSummary (avg values + has_data flag) get_cost adapter.get_cost(resource_ids, days) dict[resource_id, float] (USD) get_last_activity adapter.get_last_activity(resource_id, resource_type) ISO8601 timestamp or null submit_findings (none — ends the loop) Structured findings for the report

docs.title: Token optimization
docs.text:
Three mechanisms keep AI token usage low:

  1. Non-billable resource filter — IAM roles, subnets, route tables, CloudFormation stacks, etc. are stripped before the AI sees list_resources. Cuts 60–70% of resources in a typical account.
  2. Compact JSON — resource list uses short keys (id, type, region) and omits null fields. No whitespace in serialized JSON.
  3. Prompt caching (Anthropic API provider) — the system prompt is pinned with cache_control: ephemeral, so iterations 2–N are billed at the cached-read rate for that portion.

docs.title: Finding lifecycle
docs.text:
Resource Explorer / Asset Inventory / Resource Graph
        ↓ filter non-billable + EXCLUDE_TAGS / EXCLUDE_RESOURCE_TYPES
get_cost (Phase 0, one batched call, no AI tokens)
        ↓ sort by cost, keep top MAX_RESOURCES_PER_SCAN
AI sees list_resources result (compact JSON with cost_usd)
        ↓ AI prioritizes expensive candidates
get_metrics + get_last_activity (per candidate, parallel)
        ↓ AI reasons: idle? underutilized? orphaned?
submit_findings
        ↓
ResourceFinding dataclass list
        ↓
build_report() → JSON report (+ scan_diff vs previous scan)
        ↓
build_board_html() → self-contained decision board
        ↓ (if REPORT_S3_BUCKET / REPORT_GCS_BUCKET / REPORT_STORAGE_ACCOUNT is set)
upload to S3 / GCS / Azure Blob → pre-signed / SAS URL
        ↓ (if REMEDIATION_ENABLED=true)
run_remediation() → Jira tickets for policy matches
        ↓
build notification payload
        ↓
notify_all() → delivers to each channel in NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER

docs.title: Opportunities
docs.text:
A scan can return hundreds of findings. Nobody decides about 499 things one by one, so Argus groups findings into opportunities: a short list of decisions, each with one action, a savings range, and the full list of resources behind it. The grouping is deterministic. No model is involved, so two runs on the same findings always give the same opportunities.

Prototype

Opportunities are in the JSON report (opportunities, opportunity_summary), in python -m core.opportunities and on the decision board. The Slack digest and ticket flow do not use them yet.

docs.title: How findings are grouped
docs.text:
The key is action x resource family x tier.

Part Values How it is decided Action remove, stop, rightsize, retention, review Rule findings are removals. Otherwise the first verb in the recommendation decides ("delete", "terminate", "release" are remove; "right-size", "downsize" are rightsize; "review", "verify", "confirm" are review). No verb means review Family the resource type, except all snapshot types share snapshot Tier flagged, unsure, sure flagged when the finding needs human review (production-like name or large unbilled estimate); unsure when its confidence is low or missing; otherwise sure. One doubtful member therefore cannot keep a whole group out of the easy lane

Owners are not part of the key. Splitting by owner multiplied the group count by more than two on a real scan. Each opportunity lists its top five owners (from the team, owner, project, application or service tag, in that order) and how many members have none.

docs.title: Small groups and the cap
docs.text: Groups smaller than min_group_size (default 2) collapse into one other resources opportunity per action and tier. If the list still has more than max_opportunities (default 50), the minimum is raised until it fits. Every finding is in exactly one opportunity, so totals never double count.

docs.title: Lanes
docs.text:
Lane Meaning easy action is remove, stop or retention, and the tier is sure doubt everything else: review and rightsize actions, unsure and flagged tiers

Easy opportunities are listed first, then by savings.

docs.title: Savings range
docs.text:
Field Meaning low_usd billed plus list-priced dollars: deterministic figures high_usd low_usd plus the model's estimates, taken at face value by_basis dollars per cost_basis unpriced members with no dollar figure; they are not in either bound

The two bounds add up to the report's total_estimated_waste_usd (high) and to its billed and list-priced part (low).

docs.title: Stable ids and related links
docs.text:
id is a hash of the key, so the same kind of opportunity keeps its id from one scan to the next. Decisions recorded against an id therefore survive new scans.

related lists other opportunities whose findings name one of this opportunity's resource ids in their reasoning (for example a stopped instance that mentions its disk). It is a hint to check for overlap, not a guarantee.

docs.title: Measuring a report
docs.text:
python -m core.opportunities summary --report local_reports/aws/<date>/<scan>.json
python -m core.opportunities summary --report <scan>.json --list 10

Without --list only counts and dollars are printed, never resource names. --min-group-size and --max-opportunities override the defaults.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The action comes from keywords in the recommendation text, so an unusual phrasing falls back to review.
  • Relations between resources are found by id mentions only.
  • Titles are plain templates. Richer text and risk notes come later.

docs.title: Quick contribution guide
docs.text:
1. Fork the repo and create a branch
  2. Make your changes
  3. Run pytest tests/ -v — all tests must pass
  4. Run ruff format . && ruff check . (CI checks both)
  5. Open a PR against main

docs.title: PR checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] All existing tests pass (pytest tests/ -v)
  • [ ] New code has tests
  • [ ] Type hints on all public functions
  • [ ] No real cloud credentials or API keys in any file
  • [ ] ARCHITECTURE.md and the relevant docs/ pages updated if behavior or architecture changed

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • git

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/vamshisiddarth/argus.git
cd argus
python3.11 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pip install pre-commit    # not included in the dev extra
pre-commit install

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
All tests run offline — no cloud credentials needed:

pytest tests/ -v                   # unit tests (integration tests are excluded by default)
make test-integration              # integration tests only (pytest -m integration)
make test-all                      # everything

Subsets:

pytest tests/adapters/aws/ -v     # AWS adapter
pytest tests/adapters/gcp/ -v     # GCP adapter
pytest tests/adapters/azure/ -v   # Azure adapter
pytest tests/ai/ -v               # AI providers
pytest tests/core/ -v             # Agent loop, chat session, report generation, remediation engine
pytest tests/integrations/ -v     # Jira tracker
pytest tests/entrypoints/ -v      # CLI and runtime entrypoints

With coverage:

pytest tests/ --cov=. --cov-report=term-missing

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
Pre-commit hooks run ruff (lint + format) and mypy automatically on each commit. To set them up:

pre-commit install          # one-time setup
pre-commit run --all-files  # manual run on all files

You can also run the tools directly:

ruff format .     # format
ruff check .      # lint
ruff check --fix  # auto-fix lint issues
mypy core/ adapters/ ai/ entrypoints/ --ignore-missing-imports --no-warn-unused-ignores   # same as CI

Rules: - Line length: 88 characters - Type hints on all public functions - No bare except Exception, except in top-level runners that must never block delivery (marked # noqa: BLE001)

CI runs ruff format --check ., ruff check ., mypy, the test suite on Python 3.11–3.13, and a strict docs build. Note that the Makefile's lint / fmt targets still call black; CI uses ruff format, so prefer the commands above. - Python 3.11+ minimum (match, | union types freely; avoid 3.12+ type statement)

docs.title: Running the docs site locally

pip install mkdocs-material mkdocs-minify-plugin mike   # already included in the dev extra
mkdocs serve

Open http://localhost:8000.
